title: At the Limits of Computability: Steps Towards Autonomous AI Discovery on the Busy Beaver Frontier
content:

Title:At the Limits of Computability: Steps Towards Autonomous AI Discovery on the Busy Beaver Frontier
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Recent breakthroughs in AI for mathematics---ranging from Olympiad medal performances to resolving long-standing open conjectures---have rapidly expanded what automated systems can achieve. Yet these successes primarily concern predefined, human-formulated problems, leaving open how AI systems can autonomously uncover mathematical structure and formulate new questions. To push beyond static challenges, we explore the Busy Beaver (BB) domain, an uncomputable frontier that is fundamentally open-ended. Because no algorithm can compute the Busy Beaver number $\mathrm{BB}(n)$ for every $n$, this domain provides a natural setting for sustained exploration through mathematical conjecture and proof. In this paper, we introduce a Gemini-based agentic pipeline that automatically discovers accelerations of Turing machines, expressed as compact mathematical rules summarizing many execution steps. Our system integrates pattern recognition, automated conjecturing, informal mathematical reasoning, and formal theorem proving in Lean. With this framework, our system autonomously discovered and formally verified novel Collatz-like accelerations for eleven machines in $\mathrm{BB}(6)$. Subject to community acceptance, we provisionally classify these machines as Cryptids, namely machines whose blank-tape executions admit exact, compact mathematical descriptions but whose halting behavior remains unresolved. These results advance the analysis of $\mathrm{BB}(6)$ holdouts on the Busy Beaver frontier and demonstrate the potential of autonomous AI systems for open-ended mathematical discovery in fundamental computer science.

report.summary: A Gemini-based AI agent autonomously discovered and formally verified Collatz-like acceleration rules for eleven Busy Beaver machines, advancing open-ended mathematical discovery at the limits of computability.
report.background: The Busy Beaver function asks for the maximum number of steps an n-state Turing machine can run on a blank tape before halting. It is uncomputable: no algorithm can compute BB(n) for every n, and the function grows faster than any computable function. BB(6) is a current frontier with many 'holdouts'—machines whose halting behavior remains unresolved. Researchers seek 'accelerations': compact mathematical rules that summarize enormous numbers of execution steps, often with Collatz-like structure. AI for mathematics has recently scored high-profile wins on Olympiad problems and open conjectures, but mostly on human-formulated targets. This paper tests whether an AI agent can autonomously find mathematical structure in a fundamentally open-ended, uncomputable domain.
key_points: The system is a Gemini-based agentic pipeline that combines pattern recognition, automated conjecture generation, informal mathematical reasoning, and formal theorem proving in Lean. Rather than solving a fixed benchmark, it searches for compact 'accelerations' that summarize many Turing-machine execution steps as mathematical rules.

The agent autonomously discovered and formally verified novel Collatz-like accelerations for eleven machines in BB(6). The authors provisionally call these machines 'Cryptids': their blank-tape runs admit exact, compact mathematical descriptions, yet their halting behavior remains unresolved. Community acceptance is still pending.

The work shifts AI-for-math from predefined problem solving toward open-ended discovery. Because Busy Beaver is uncomputable, no system can exhaust the domain; progress depends on conjecture, proof, and human-AI collaboration. The pipeline shows agents can generate mathematically meaningful structure and check it formally, not just produce plausible text.

Formal verification in Lean is a key guardrail: it confirms the discovered acceleration rules are correct, but it does not settle whether the machines halt. The BB(6) frontier remains open. The result is best read as a proof of concept for autonomous mathematical exploration, not a solution to the halting problem or a complete classification of BB(6).
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a signal that agentic systems paired with proof assistants can tackle open-ended scientific discovery, not just benchmarks. It could accelerate work in automated theorem proving, program analysis, and trustworthy AI reasoning, where formal checks matter. For developers, the recipe—pattern mining, conjecture generation, and Lean verification—is a template for building research agents; the hard parts are search control, domain knowledge, and human curation. For regular users, the near-term effect is indirect: better AI assistants for technical reasoning and more reliable verification, not a tool that solves uncomputable problems. Expect more pilots in mathematics and formal methods.
report.tools: Follow Lean 4 and Mathlib for formal proofs; the Busy Beaver Challenge (bbchallenge.org) for BB(6) holdouts, deciders, and community discussion of Cryptids; Gemini API or open agent frameworks such as LangGraph or AutoGen for agentic pipelines; and proof-automation projects like AlphaProof as reference points. Watch the paper's artifact and any released acceleration rules.
